query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing heavy Hf with additional Ti in the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the alloy’s density while preserving its strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and high mechanical strength at room and high temperatures
generation.intervention: Introduce a partial substitution of Hf by increasing the Ti content (i.e., form a modified composition with lower Hf and proportionally higher Ti) while keeping the overall phase stability and BCC structure intact.
generation.conditions: Mechanical loading and testing at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The alteration of the elemental composition maintains a single solid solution (likely BCC) where the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening are preserved despite the reduced average atomic weight.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the proportion of heavy Hf and increasing the lighter Ti, the alloy’s overall density is decreased. Simultaneously, the Ti addition supports solid solution strengthening and phase stability (as supported by studies on Ti-rich alloys), ensuring minimal loss in mechanical performance. This leverages the known effect that Ti (and Zr) additions can lower density adequately while still contributing to the elevated-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the original alloy, the modified alloy is expected to show a reduced density (potentially a reduction in the range of 5-10%) with little to no degradation in yield strength or ductility at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Performance data of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (density ~10.21 g/cm³ and high mechanical performance at both ambient and ~1000 °C conditions).
generation.boundary: Findings are applicable under the conditions of as-cast microstructures, with testing in the temperature range from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C and under comparable mechanical loading regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal level of Hf substitution by Ti is not yet quantified, and the precise balance between density reduction and strength retention requires experimental calibration. There is uncertainty in the exact percentage reduction in density and potential minor changes in mechanical properties that must be empirically verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloy samples in which Hf is incrementally replaced by Ti (for example, 10%, 20%, and 30% substitution by atomic percentage) while keeping the ratios of Mo, Ta, and Zr constant. Process the alloys using the same as-cast procedures and perform structural characterization (e.g., XRD to confirm single-phase BCC structure). Then carry out mechanical tests (tensile/compression) at room temperature and at 1000 °C, and measure the density of each sample.
measurements: Yield strength (MPa) at room temperature and ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any of the substituted alloys exhibits a density reduction of less than approximately 5% compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if there is a statistically significant (e.g., >10-15%) reduction in yield strength or ductility at either room temperature or ~1000 °C compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen

Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility).
